topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-1's definition of 'Firm,' which of the following business entity forms may a Georgia real estate brokerage lawfully operate as?
choice_a: Only a corporation; other entity forms are not permitted to hold a firm license
choice_b: A corporation, partnership, limited liability company, or sole proprietorship -- the statute defines 'Firm' broadly to include, but not be limited to, all of these entity forms
choice_c: Only a sole proprietorship; corporate brokerages are prohibited in Georgia
choice_d: Only a limited liability company; partnerships and corporations are excluded
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-1 defines 'Firm' as any business entity, including but not limited to a corporation, partnership, limited liability company, or sole proprietorship -- meaning a Georgia brokerage can lawfully be organized under any of these common business-entity forms.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: What does O.C.G.A. § 43-40-9 require of a business entity (Firm) before its affiliated members, officers, or employees can be licensed to act under it, including a nonresident corporation or LLC seeking to do business in Georgia?
choice_a: Only the individual salespersons need to be licensed; the Firm itself never needs to hold any license
choice_b: Nonresident corporations and LLCs are categorically barred from qualifying for a Georgia broker's license under any circumstances
choice_c: The Firm itself must first qualify for a broker's license before affiliated individuals can be licensed under it
choice_d: A Firm need only register its trade name with the Secretary of State; no broker's license is required at the entity level
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-9 requires that a Firm -- including a nonresident corporation or LLC -- qualify for a broker's license before its affiliated members, officers, or employees can be licensed to act under that Firm, establishing that entity-level licensure is a prerequisite to individual affiliation.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: What is the GREC-recognized term for the broker designated as responsible for a Georgia real estate Firm, referenced in O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25 among the licensees subject to discipline?
explanation: 'Qualifying broker' is confirmed, real Georgia terminology -- O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25 references 'a broker, qualifying broker, or associate broker' among licensees subject to discipline, and § 43-40-9 confirms that a Firm must qualify for a broker's license, i.e., have a broker attached to it in this role.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: Consistent with Georgia's statutory scheme requiring every Firm to have a broker attached to it as qualifying broker, which of the following is the well-established understanding of who may serve in that role?
choice_a: Only a licensed broker, not a salesperson, is understood to be eligible to serve as a firm's qualifying broker, consistent with the overall statutory scheme even though this specific point is treated as established practice rather than a directly quotable rule citation
choice_b: Either a broker or a salesperson may serve as a firm's qualifying broker interchangeably under the statute
choice_c: Any individual holding any Georgia professional license, including outside real estate, may serve as a firm's qualifying broker
choice_d: A firm need not designate any qualifying broker as long as all of its affiliated licensees are salespersons
explanation: Because the statutory scheme requires a Firm to have a broker attached to it as qualifying broker, it follows -- as well-established industry and regulatory understanding consistent with that scheme -- that a salesperson, who lacks broker licensure, is not eligible to serve as a firm's qualifying broker; this specific limitation is treated here as established practice rather than a directly quoted rule citation.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: What does a firm's requirement to have a qualifying broker attached to it, under O.C.G.A. §§ 43-40-9 and 43-40-25, primarily establish?
choice_a: That only sole proprietorships require a qualifying broker; other entity forms are exempt
choice_b: That regardless of which business-entity form (corporation, partnership, LLC, or sole proprietorship) a firm chooses under § 43-40-1, it must have a broker designated as responsible for the firm before affiliated licensees can operate under it
choice_c: That the qualifying broker requirement applies only to firms with more than ten affiliated licensees
choice_d: That a qualifying broker is required only for firms engaged exclusively in property management
explanation: Read together, §§ 43-40-1, 43-40-9, and 43-40-25 establish that whatever business-entity form a Georgia real estate firm takes, it must have a broker attached to it as qualifying broker before affiliated members/officers/employees can be licensed to act under that firm -- the entity-form choice does not eliminate this requirement.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: As a general matter of business-entity law, what is a key distinction between a general partnership and a limited partnership?
choice_a: A limited partnership can have only one partner total, while a general partnership requires at least three
choice_b: General partnerships are always taxed as corporations, while limited partnerships are never subject to any taxation
choice_c: In a general partnership, all partners typically share management responsibility and unlimited personal liability, while a limited partnership includes at least one limited partner whose liability is generally restricted to their investment and who typically does not participate in day-to-day management
choice_d: There is no meaningful distinction between the two structures under general business-entity law
explanation: Under general business-entity doctrine, a general partnership involves partners who typically share both management authority and unlimited personal liability, while a limited partnership includes at least one limited partner whose liability is generally capped at their investment and who generally does not participate in day-to-day management, in exchange for that limited-liability protection.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: As a general matter of business-entity law, what is a key liability distinction between operating as a limited liability company (LLC) and operating as a corporation?
choice_a: An LLC provides no liability protection at all, while only a corporation can ever limit owner liability
choice_b: A corporation can never have more than one shareholder, while an LLC has no limit on members
choice_c: LLCs are legally prohibited from operating a real estate brokerage business in any state
choice_d: Both generally provide their owners limited liability protection, but they typically differ in formalities, management flexibility, and default tax treatment rather than in the basic concept of limiting owner liability
explanation: Both LLCs and corporations are generally recognized business-entity forms designed to provide their owners limited liability protection (subject to state-law formalities being observed), but they typically differ in governance formality, management flexibility, and default tax treatment rather than in whether liability protection exists at all.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: As a general matter of business-entity law, what distinguishes a sole proprietorship from a corporation or LLC with respect to owner liability?
choice_a: A sole proprietorship exposes its owner to unlimited personal liability for business debts and obligations, while a corporation or properly maintained LLC is generally designed to shield the owner's personal assets beyond their investment in the business
choice_b: A sole proprietorship automatically shields the owner from all personal liability, identical to a corporation
choice_c: Sole proprietorships are legally required to have at least two owners
choice_d: Corporations and LLCs expose their owners to greater personal liability than a sole proprietorship
explanation: A sole proprietorship is the simplest business form -- one individual operates the business with no separate legal entity, so the owner bears unlimited personal liability -- whereas a corporation or a properly maintained LLC is a separate legal entity generally designed to limit the owner's exposure to their investment in the business.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: Which of the following describes 'price-fixing' as an antitrust violation relevant to real estate brokerage practice?
choice_a: A single brokerage's unilateral decision to set its own commission rate without input from any competitor
choice_b: An agreement between competing brokers or firms to set, fix, or standardize commission rates or fees rather than each independently determining its own pricing
choice_c: A government agency's regulation of licensing fees
choice_d: A buyer negotiating a lower commission rate directly with their own agent
explanation: Price-fixing is an antitrust violation involving an agreement between competitors -- such as competing brokers or firms -- to set, fix, or standardize prices or fees like commission rates, rather than each competitor independently determining its own pricing; a single firm's unilateral pricing decision is not price-fixing.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: What is a 'group boycott' in the antitrust context as it applies to real estate brokerage practice?
choice_a: A single brokerage's independent decision not to accept a particular listing
choice_b: A government-imposed moratorium on new construction in a designated area
choice_c: An agreement among two or more competing firms to refuse to deal with, or to work with, a particular competitor, client, or other market participant in order to disadvantage them
choice_d: A homeowners association's vote to reject a proposed zoning variance
explanation: A group boycott occurs when two or more competing firms agree to collectively refuse to deal with, or work with, a targeted competitor, client, or other market participant, which is distinguished from a single firm's independent business decision -- unilateral refusals to deal generally do not raise the same antitrust concern as concerted action.
source_note: hedge: standard national content -- antitrust law as applied to real estate practice

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: What is 'market allocation' as an antitrust violation relevant to real estate brokerage competition?
choice_a: A single firm's decision to specialize in a particular price range or neighborhood without any agreement with competitors
choice_b: A zoning ordinance that separates residential and commercial districts
choice_c: A brokerage's advertising campaign targeting a specific demographic
choice_d: An agreement among competing firms to divide up territories, customer types, or price ranges among themselves rather than competing for the same business
explanation: Market allocation is an antitrust violation in which competing firms agree to divide markets among themselves -- by geographic territory, customer type, or price range -- so that each competitor has an effectively exclusive segment rather than genuinely competing, which is unlawful precisely because it is a concerted agreement rather than independent business strategy.
source_note: hedge: standard national content -- antitrust law as applied to real estate practice

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: What is a 'tie-in arrangement' (tying) as an antitrust concern relevant to real estate brokerage practice?
choice_a: Conditioning the provision of one service or product on the client's agreement to also purchase a separate, distinct service or product from the same provider or an affiliate
choice_b: A brokerage offering multiple unrelated services that a client may choose to purchase independently of one another
choice_c: A referral made with the client's full knowledge and voluntary consent to an unaffiliated service provider
choice_d: A standard multiple listing service cooperation agreement between competing brokerages
explanation: A tie-in (tying) arrangement raises antitrust concern when a provider conditions the sale of one product or service on the buyer also purchasing a separate, distinct product or service -- for example, requiring a client to use an affiliated mortgage or title company as a condition of brokerage representation -- as opposed to services being independently offered and chosen.
source_note: hedge: standard national content -- antitrust law as applied to real estate practice

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: What is the general purpose of the national Do-Not-Call List in the context of real estate licensee marketing and prospecting?
choice_a: It bars all real estate advertising in any medium, including print and online
choice_b: It restricts telemarketing calls to consumers who have registered their phone numbers to opt out of most unsolicited sales calls, with limited exceptions such as an existing business relationship
choice_c: It applies only to commercial businesses and has no bearing on individual licensee prospecting calls
choice_d: It requires licensees to call every number on the list at least once per year
explanation: The national Do-Not-Call Registry allows consumers to opt out of most unsolicited telemarketing calls, and real estate licensees engaged in cold-call prospecting must generally check registered numbers and comply with applicable exceptions (such as an existing business relationship) before calling, or risk regulatory penalties.
source_note: hedge: standard national content -- federal Do-Not-Call compliance

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: What is a generally sound practice for a licensee's use of social media and internet advertising to promote listings and services?
choice_a: Social media posts are entirely exempt from any advertising standards that apply to other marketing channels
choice_b: A licensee's personal social media account is never considered business advertising, regardless of its content
choice_c: Ensuring posted content is accurate and not misleading, and that required identifying/brokerage information and applicable advertising disclosures are included, consistent with general advertising-accuracy obligations that apply across all marketing channels
choice_d: Only paid social media advertisements are subject to any accuracy or disclosure standards
explanation: General advertising-accuracy obligations extend to social media and internet marketing just as they do to traditional advertising -- licensees should ensure content is accurate and not misleading and include required identifying/brokerage information, since the medium does not exempt the content from applicable standards.
source_note: hedge: standard national content -- advertising practice guidance across marketing channels

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: Why is protecting a client's confidential personal information (such as financial details or Social Security numbers collected during a transaction) an important general licensee responsibility?
choice_a: Because confidential personal information collected during a transaction has no ongoing relevance once the transaction closes
choice_b: Because only lenders, never real estate licensees, ever handle a client's sensitive personal information
choice_c: Because sharing client financial information with third parties is always permitted as long as it helps close the transaction faster
choice_d: Because mishandling or improperly disclosing sensitive personal information can expose clients to identity theft or fraud and can expose the licensee/firm to liability, making careful data-handling and confidentiality practices part of a licensee's general due-diligence responsibilities
explanation: Real estate transactions often involve sensitive personal and financial information; general due-diligence and ethical practice call for licensees to safeguard this information against improper disclosure, since mishandling it can expose clients to identity theft or fraud and expose the licensee and firm to liability.
source_note: hedge: standard national content -- data/confidentiality due-diligence practice

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: In general terms, what does a licensee's 'due diligence responsibility' mean in the context of representing a client in a real estate transaction?
choice_a: A general obligation to reasonably investigate, verify, and disclose material information relevant to the transaction rather than passing along unverified claims or ignoring obvious red flags
choice_b: An obligation limited strictly to verifying the buyer's identification document at the initial meeting
choice_c: A one-time requirement satisfied entirely by having the client sign an agency disclosure form
choice_d: A responsibility that applies only to brokers, never to individual salespersons
explanation: Due diligence in this context broadly refers to a licensee's general obligation to reasonably investigate, verify, and disclose material information relevant to a transaction -- rather than simply relaying unverified claims from another party or ignoring red flags -- as part of competent, ethical representation.
source_note: hedge: standard national content -- general due-diligence practice

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: A group of brokers in the same market informally agree among themselves to each charge the same standard commission percentage rather than competing on price. What antitrust concern does this most directly raise?
choice_a: Market allocation, because the brokers are dividing geographic territory among themselves
choice_b: Price-fixing, because it is an agreement between competitors to set or standardize pricing rather than each firm independently determining its own commission rate
choice_c: Tying, because the brokers are conditioning one service on the purchase of another
choice_d: This raises no antitrust concern because commission rates are always set by state regulators, not brokers
explanation: An agreement among competing brokers to standardize commission rates rather than set them independently is a textbook example of price-fixing, an antitrust violation, precisely because it replaces independent competitive pricing decisions with a concerted agreement among competitors.
